analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their families from buying individual stocks and requires advance public notice before sales.
analysis.headline: 16 Republican senators backed the bill, but it has sat in the Senate Homeland Security Committee with no action since its March 2026 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children from buying individual stocks or stock derivatives while in office. Any sale of a stock they still hold would have to be announced publicly at least 7 days before it happens. Violators would pay a fee and give up any profits on trades that broke the rules, and they could not pay the fee out of their official office accounts or campaign funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans get a government whose lawmakers are less able to trade on information only insiders have. Members themselves would keep broad index funds and diversified mutual funds, and could still hold existing stocks, but new purchases of individual companies would be off-limits.

how_it_helps.text: Bars members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children from purchasing individual stocks of publicly traded companies or any derivative tied to them while in office.
Requires public notice, filed with the House Clerk or Senate Secretary and posted online, at least 7 and not more than 14 days before any sale of a covered stock by a member or their family.

Exempts diversified investment funds, interests in small businesses, and blind trusts where the member has no say over specific investments — so members can invest broadly without leaving public markets.

Requires violators to sell any stock bought in violation and pay a fee of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade's value, plus any net gains, and bars paying the fee from office allowances or campaign funds.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their families, who would lose the ability to buy individual stocks and would have to publicly announce planned sales of holdings they keep. The restriction also applies to spouses and dependent children, which limits household investment choices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their families

drawbacks.text: Members may keep individual stocks they already own indefinitely; the bill only requires public notice before selling them, so it stops new purchases but does not force divestment of existing holdings.

The required advance public notice of a sale is itself published to the markets 7 to 14 days before the trade, which could let outsiders react to a member's planned sale — a tradeoff the bill accepts rather than solving.
Enforcement is a fee, not a criminal penalty: a violator pays money and must divest, with a criminal referral possible only if a member resigns or retires without paying an assessed fee.

Exceptions are broad: spouses and children can transact for employers or in fiduciary roles, and trusts count as exempt as long as the member cannot direct specific decisions and the trustee is not a close relative — lines that depend on case-by-case judgment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — lawmakers with fewer chances to trade on nonpublic information — is real, and the cost to members is one they can absorb through diversified funds. The bill is a middle path: stricter than current law, but weaker than proposals that require full divestiture of all individual stocks, and its penalty structure is financial rather than criminal. Honest supporters would acknowledge it leaves existing holdings untouched and leans on ethics offices for enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Sen. Pete Ricketts introduced the bill in the Senate on March 18, 2026, joined by six original cosponsors — Sens. McCormick, Husted, Fischer, Marshall, Cassidy, and Young.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
The bill has 15 cosponsors, all Republicans, and no Democratic cosponsor.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the bill's action history after the committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, members of Congress keep their current ability to buy and sell individual stocks, since the bill has not advanced past a committee referral.

for.name: Sen. Pete Ricketts
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Insider Trading Act in the Senate and led its introduction with six Republican colleagues.

for.name: 15 Republican Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill, making its support entirely from one party.

against.name: Sen. Rand Paul
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, has taken no action on the bill; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since the March 2026 referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 senators supporting the bill are Republicans and no Democrat has cosponsored, but no vote has occurred, so the full partisan split is unknown.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their households
industries.note: The bill removes their ability to buy individual stocks and derivatives and requires public notice before selling existing holdings, with fees and divestment for violations. Their interest in keeping flexible, information-advantaged trading runs against the public's interest in lawmakers without trading conflicts.

analysis.trajectory: Congressional stock-trading ban bills have repeatedly stalled in committee in recent Congresses, and this one has all its support from one party with no committee action since March 2026. Unless the Homeland Security committee schedules a markup before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, the bill will die without a vote.
